idiom_name: createX(options) factory function returning an object literal or closure
implementation_notes: JavaScript's native realization is a plain function that decides what to build and returns an object literal or a closure over private state - no classes, no `new`, no prototype chain needed. MDN notes that a class with only a constructor is not much different from a createX factory function, and Object.create shows the same idea one level lower. Because a function can return anything, it can return a cached instance, a frozen configuration object, or a different shape per input, which a constructor cannot.
pitfalls: Methods defined inside the literal are fresh per instance; if thousands of objects are built, put shared methods on a prototype (Object.create(PROTO) or a class) instead.
Closures keep the constructor arguments alive; a factory that captures large inputs can retain far more memory than the returned object suggests.
Returning objects of different shapes per branch creates polymorphic call sites that deoptimize; keep a stable shape (same keys in the same order) for performance-sensitive factories.

variants.name: Static create() on a class hierarchy
variants.idiom_name: static create() selecting a subclass; Object.create/Promise.resolve precedent
variants.implementation_notes: When subclassing is genuinely wanted, the classic structure survives as a static method on the base class that picks the concrete subclass (the same shape the standard library uses with Object.create and Promise.resolve). The caller writes Shape.create(kind) and never touches `new`; private fields and subclass hooks remain available. It is the right choice when products are classes with behaviour and instanceof/extends matter, and the wrong choice for plain data.
pitfalls: Static methods are inherited but freeze the receiver at call time: Shape.create inside a subclass still refers to Shape, so dispatch cannot vary per subclass the way a virtual create() can.
A class whose constructor is documented as private is still callable in JavaScript unless you throw or use private fields to enforce the factory; the restriction is documentation, not syntax.
Derived-class constructors must call super() before using this; a factory that returns a subclass instance built by a helper must respect that ordering.
